entry.title: Post Quantum Recovery Framework
entry.summary:
The prospect of a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) poses a significant challenge to the security foundations of Bitcoin, particularly those built on elliptic curve cryptography. Should such a computer be realized, it would threaten the integrity of existing coins unless proactive measures—such as activating post-quantum (PQ) output types and migrating funds—have been taken in advance. However, not all users may complete this migration, highlighting the necessity for a Post-Quantum Recovery Protocol to safeguard remaining assets.
A PQ recovery scheme involves implementing consensus changes that add new spending conditions to pre-existing unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs), aiming to protect them from theft if elliptic curve security is compromised. These schemes can be categorized as either Prepared or Unprepared. Prepared recovery requires action or data commitment before the hypothetical "Q-day" when quantum computers become capable of breaking current cryptographic assumptions. By contrast, Unprepared recovery assumes no prior user action and is designed to work independently of the specific PQ output type chosen, thus providing broader applicability across the network.
To design an effective recovery protocol, it is essential to distinguish between the "what" and the "how." The "what" refers to the recovery secret—the key information a user must possess, which could range from public keys obscured by hashes to private seeds or passphrases. The "how" pertains to the mechanisms used to leverage this secret into a valid transaction that moves funds to a secure location. Recovery methods include commit/reveal protocols, such as dropkick and lifeboat, and zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) protocols that keep the recovery secret concealed. These approaches can often be combined interchangeably, though certain technical nuances might constrain their compatibility.
Recovery secrets themselves fall into two main categories: accidental and essential. Accidental secrets are data like public keys and scripts that, while not immediately conferring control over coins, can be revealed without compromising security as long as elliptic curve cryptography remains reliable. Examples include pubkeys hidden behind hashed output types (e.g., P2PKH, P2WPKH, P2SH, P2WSH), BIP32 extended public keys (xpubs), and internal keys or scripts associated with P2TR outputs. Essential secrets, by contrast, directly confer ownership—examples being BIP32 seeds, brainwallet passphrases, or other private scalar preimages. While most modern wallets use BIP39 seed phrases to generate BIP32 master keys, any deviation from this standard could introduce new risks.
A significant dilemma arises in choosing between these types of recovery secrets. Relying solely on essential secrets like BIP32 derivation paths risks rendering some coins permanently inaccessible, especially those created before BIP32 existed or where provenance cannot be proven. Conversely, depending only on accidental secrets exposes coins to potential theft, as public keys and scripts are sometimes shared outside the blockchain context, making them accessible to malicious actors. This trade-off is more philosophical than technical, as it involves weighing the destruction of some coins against the possibility of others being stolen.
One proposed mitigation is the concept of "recovery eras," wherein the requirements for spending UTXOs change over time. For example, in the initial period after Q-day, only transactions proven using essential secrets would be permitted, giving diligent users a window to reclaim their coins safely. After this period, accidental secrets could become valid for recovery, enabling those who lack essential secrets to access their funds while accepting increased risk of theft. Alternatively, these eras could be dynamic, tied to each UTXO's age, offering longer protection to older, less frequently moved coins.
Multisignature (multisig) outputs introduce additional complexity. In traditional M-of-N multisig arrangements, requiring accidental secrets effectively reduces the security threshold, possibly allowing one co-signer to act alone. Insisting on essential secrets heightens the risk of rendering coins inaccessible if even one participant cannot provide their part. Given that multisig inherently involves some degree of intra-group trust, using accidental secrets for recovery may be acceptable in many cases, but the debate ultimately revolves around whether to prioritize preventing theft among co-signers or preserving access to funds.
In sum, while post-quantum recovery protocols can offer robust protections for most Bitcoin holdings, they must balance the conflicting goals of minimizing both theft and destruction. These solutions will not only need to withstand future advances in quantum computing but also navigate the complexities of reaching consensus within the community. Continued development and discussion are critical to refining these protocols and ensuring that Bitcoin remains resilient—even in the face of unprecedented computational threats. For further reading on related commit/reveal techniques such as shrinc-ray, interested readers can explore [shrinc-ray](https://gist.github.com/ajtowns/d6bfc7a2fa4a2fdfe9f8f79cf1e1db34).
